passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of caffeine on reaction time in a controlled laboratory setting. A total of 120 healthy adults aged 18–35 were randomly assigned to one of four groups: (1) placebo, (2) low-dose caffeine (50 mg), (3) medium-dose caffeine (100 mg), and (4) high-dose caffeine (200 mg). Each participant performed a simple visual-motor task that required pressing a button as soon as a light appeared on a screen. Reaction times were recorded in milliseconds. The mean reaction times and standard deviations for each group were as follows: Placebo: 350 ms (± 30 ms); Low-dose: 330 ms (± 28 ms); Medium-dose: 310 ms (± 25 ms); High-dose: 305 ms (± 27 ms). The researchers noted that reaction time decreased with increasing caffeine dose up to 100 mg, after which the improvement plateaued. They concluded that moderate caffeine intake improves cognitive performance but that higher doses offer diminishing returns.
stem: Which of the following best describes the trend observed in reaction times across the caffeine dose groups?

options.A: Reaction time increases with higher caffeine doses.
options.B: Reaction time decreases linearly with higher caffeine doses.
options.C: Reaction time decreases up to 100 mg and then plateaus.
options.D: Reaction time remains unchanged across all doses.

explanation: The data show a decrease in mean reaction time from placebo to 100 mg, after which the reduction is minimal (from 310 ms to 305 ms), indicating a plateau.
trap: Option B suggests a linear decrease, which would predict a larger drop from 100 mg to 200 mg, not observed.

stem: Which additional group would best test whether reaction time keeps improving at doses above those studied, changing only the dose?

options.A: A 400 mg caffeine group performing the same task
options.B: A 100 mg caffeine group performing a memory task
options.C: A placebo group tested at a different time of day
options.D: A 50 mg caffeine group with twice the sample size

explanation: Correct: A 400 mg group with the same task extends the dose range and changes only the dose. Why the others are wrong: B) it changes the task as well as repeating a tested dose. C) it changes the time of day and adds no information above 200 mg. D) it repeats a tested dose and says nothing about higher doses.
trap: Choosing a group that changes the task or time of day, or repeats a tested dose, instead of extending the dose range alone.

stem: Assuming the standard deviation remains constant, what is the approximate 95% confidence interval for the mean reaction time of the high-dose group?
explanation: Correct: SE = 27/√30 ≈ 4.93 ms; 95% CI ≈ mean ± 1.96 × SE ≈ 305 ± 9.7, about ±10 ms. Why the others are wrong: A) ±5 ms is roughly one SE, not the 95% margin. C) ±12 ms overestimates the margin. D) ±20 ms is far too wide for n = 30.
trap: Reporting one standard error (about 5 ms) as the 95% margin instead of roughly two standard errors.

stem: Which of the following statements could be a potential confounding factor in this study?

options.A: All participants were instructed to avoid caffeine for 24 hours before the experiment.
options.B: The researchers used a double-blind design.
options.C: Participants varied in their habitual caffeine consumption.
options.D: The reaction time task was administered at the same time of day for all participants.

explanation: Baseline caffeine tolerance can influence reaction time, making habitual consumption a confounder if not controlled.
trap: Option A is a control measure, not a confounder.

stem: What is the percent reduction in mean reaction time from the placebo group to the medium‑dose group?
explanation: Correct: (350 − 310)/350 × 100 = 11.4%. Why the others are wrong: B) 12.9% divides by the medium‑dose mean (310) instead of the placebo mean. C) 5.7% is the low‑dose reduction (20/350). D) 40% is the absolute difference in ms, not a percent.
trap: Dividing by the medium‑dose mean, or reporting the 40 ms difference as a percent.
